title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 826–828 (Night 180, continuing nights-179), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 180 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Maymūna insists that no one in these lands can match her beloved, and she and Dahnash agree to settle the matter with a wager. She takes him down into the tower and uncovers the sleeping Qamar al-Zamān; Dahnash, after gazing at the youth, grants that she cannot be blamed, but says that his own beloved is the closest likeness to him in all creation, as if the two had been cast in one mould. Furious, Maymūna strikes him with her wing and orders him on pain of fire to bring the girl at once, so that the two can be laid side by side and compared. Dahnash and Maymūna fly off and return carrying the princess, in a shift of Venetian cloth whose sleeves are embroidered with verses, and lay her beside the sleeping youth. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلثَّمَانِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-thamānīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing for-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eightieth night,
sentences.n: A round number takes a different formula: al-mūfiya li-al-thamānīn, “the one completing the eighty”, from awfā, “to make up in full”; li- marks the number it completes. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَةَ مَيْمُونَةَ قَالَتْ لِلْعِفْرِيتِ دَهْنَشَ أَنَا أَتَحَقَّقُ أَنَّهُ لَا يُوجَدُ لِمَعْشُوقِي مَثِيلٌ فِي هٰذِهِ الدِّيَارِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ʿifrītata Maymūnata qālat li-al-ʿifrīti Dahnasha anā ataḥaqqaqu annahu lā yūjadu li-maʿshūqī mathīlun fī hādhihi al-diyāri
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-she-ifrit Maymūna said to-the-ifrit Dahnash: I, I-am-certain that-it (is), not is-found for-my-beloved an-equal in these the-lands.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the she-ifrit Maymūna said to the ifrit Dahnash, “I know for certain that there is none to equal my beloved in all these lands.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the thread by repeating Maymūna's last words from the night before. li-, “to”, marks the one addressed. Dahnash is treated as a diptote, so after li- the genitive ends in -a: Dahnasha.

sentences.t: فَهَلْ أَنْتَ مَجْنُونٌ حَتَّى نَقِيسَ مَعْشُوقَتَكَ بِمَعْشُوقِي
sentences.tr: fa-hal anta majnūnun ḥattā naqīsa maʿshūqataka bi-maʿshūqī
sentences.l: So-(is it that) you (are) mad, so-that we-measure your-beloved against-my-beloved?
sentences.i: Are you mad, that we should set your beloved beside mine?”
sentences.n: hal asks a yes-or-no question. ḥattā with the subjunctive, “so that”, here “that we should”. qāsa X bi-Y, “to measure X against Y, compare X with Y”: the verb takes bi- for the thing compared with.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا بِاللّٰهِ عَلَيْكِ يَا سَيِّدَتِي امْضِي مَعِي وَانْظُرِي مَعْشُوقَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā bi-Allāhi ʿalayki yā sayyidatī imḍī maʿī wa-unẓurī maʿshūqatī
sentences.l: So-he-said to-her: By-God upon-you, O my-lady, go with-me and-look-at my-beloved,
sentences.i: He said to her, “I beg you by God, my lady, come with me and look at my beloved,
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayki, “by God (I lay it) upon you”, the usual form of an earnest plea. The shadda of اللّه is the print's own. imḍī and unẓurī are feminine imperatives, addressed to Maymūna.

sentences.t: وَأَرْجِعُ مَعَكِ وَأَنْظُرُ مَعْشُوقَكِ
sentences.tr: wa-arjiʿu maʿaki wa-anẓuru maʿshūqaki
sentences.l: and-I-return with-you and-I-look-at your-beloved.
sentences.i: and then I will come back with you and look at yours.”
sentences.n: arjiʿu and anẓuru are first-person imperfects, “I (shall) return, I (shall) look”: the second half of the bargain.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَيْمُونَةُ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ يَا مَلْعُونُ لِأَنَّكَ شَيْطَانٌ مَكَّارٌ وَلٰكِنْ لَا أَجِئُ مَعَكَ وَلَا تَجِئُ أَنْتَ مَعِي إِلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ بِرَهْنٍ وَشَرْطٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Maymūnatu lā budda min dhālika yā malʿūnu li-annaka shayṭānun makkārun wa-lākin lā ajiʾu maʿaka wa-lā tajiʾu anta maʿī illā an yakūna bi-rahnin wa-sharṭin
sentences.l: So-said to-him Maymūna: (There is) no escape from that, O cursed-one, because-you (are) a-devil wily; but not I-come with-you and-not you-come, you, with-me, except that it-be with-a-pledge and-a-condition.
sentences.i: Maymūna said to him, “It must be so, you damned wretch, for you are a wily devil: I will not go with you, nor will you come with me, unless there is a wager on it, and terms.
sentences.n: lā budda min, “there is no escaping, it must be”. The print itself marks the shadda of مكّار and الّا. makkār, “very cunning”, is an intensive form, like karrār in the previous night. اجئ and تجئ are the print's spelling of ajīʾu and tajīʾu, “I come, you come”, without the yāʾ; they are pointed as written, and the ئ is printed. rahn is a pledge, here a stake laid on the outcome; bi- is “with”: “unless it be with a stake and terms”.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ إِنْ طَلَعَتْ مَعْشُوقَتُكَ الَّتِي أَنْتَ تُحِبُّهَا وَتَتَغَالَى فِيهَا أَحْسَنَ مِنْ مَعْشُوقِي الَّذِي ذَكَرْتُهُ وَأُحِبُّهُ وَأَتَغَالَى فِيهِ فَإِنَّ ذٰلِكَ الرَّهْنَ وَالشَّرْطَ يَكُونُ لَكَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa annahu in ṭalaʿat maʿshūqatuka allatī anta tuḥibbuhā wa-tataghālā fīhā aḥsana min maʿshūqī alladhī dhakartuhu wa-uḥibbuhu wa-ataghālā fīhi fa-inna dhālika al-rahna wa-al-sharṭa yakūnu laka ʿalayya
sentences.l: And-it (is) that-it (is): if turns-out your-beloved, whom you love-her and-exalt-beyond-measure in-her, more-beautiful than my-beloved, whom I-mentioned-him and-I-love-him and-I-exalt-beyond-measure in-him, then indeed that the-pledge and-the-condition shall-be for-you against-me;
sentences.i: And the terms are these: if your beloved, the girl you love and praise beyond all bounds, turns out more beautiful than my beloved, the one I have told you of, whom I love and praise beyond all bounds, then the stake and the terms shall be yours to claim from me;
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, “to come up”, is used as “to turn out, prove to be”, and takes its predicate in the accusative like kāna: ṭalaʿat … aḥsana, “she turned out more beautiful”. This is a colloquial usage, still alive in Egyptian Arabic. taghālā fī, “to go to extremes over, to prize beyond measure”, Form VI of the root of ghāliya, “dear, costly”. The wording is built in pairs, yours and mine, sentence for sentence. laka ʿalayya, “for you against me”, the language of a debt: you have a claim on me. The shadda of عليّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ طَلَعَ مَعْشُوقِي أَحْسَنَ فَإِنَّ ذٰلِكَ الرَّهْنَ يَكُونُ لِي عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-in ṭalaʿa maʿshūqī aḥsana fa-inna dhālika al-rahna yakūnu lī ʿalayka
sentences.l: and-if turns-out my-beloved more-beautiful, then indeed that the-pledge shall-be for-me against-you.
sentences.i: and if my beloved turns out the more beautiful, the stake shall be mine to claim from you.”
sentences.n: The mirror of the clause before. The stake itself is never named.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ دَهْنَشُ يَا سَيِّدَتِي قَبِلْتُ مِنْكِ هٰذَا الشَّرْطَ وَرَضِيتُ بِهِ تَعَالَيْ مَعِي إِلَى الْجَزَائِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ʿifrītu Dahnashu yā sayyidatī qabiltu minki hādhā al-sharṭa wa-raḍītu bihi taʿālay maʿī ilā al-jazāʾiri
sentences.l: So-said to-her the-ifrit Dahnash: O my-lady, I-have-accepted from-you this the-condition and-I-am-content with-it. Come with-me to the-islands.
sentences.i: The ifrit Dahnash said to her, “My lady, I accept these terms from you and I am content with them. Come with me to the islands.”
sentences.n: raḍiya bi-, “to be content with, agree to”: the verb takes bi-. taʿālay, “come!”, the feminine of taʿāla. al-jazāʾir, “the islands”: the realm of King al-Ghayūr, “lord of the islands and the seas”. The ئ of الجزائر is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَيْمُونَةُ لَا لِأَنَّ مَوْضِعَ مَعْشُوقِي أَقْرَبُ مِنْ مَوْضِعِ مَعْشُوقَتِكَ وَهَا هُوَ تَحْتَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Maymūnatu lā li-anna mawḍiʿa maʿshūqī aqrabu min mawḍiʿi maʿshūqatika wa-hā huwa taḥtanā
sentences.l: So-said to-him Maymūna: No, because (the) place (of) my-beloved (is) nearer than (the) place (of) your-beloved, and-here he (is), beneath-us.
sentences.i: Maymūna said to him, “No: my beloved is nearer than yours. See, he lies right beneath us.
sentences.n: The shadda of لانّ is the print's own. wa-hā huwa, “and here he is”, hā drawing attention to what follows. The two ifrits are talking in the air above the tower.

sentences.t: فَانْحَدِرْ مَعِي لِتَنْظُرَ مَعْشُوقِي وَنَرُوحَ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ إِلَى مَعْشُوقَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-inḥadir maʿī li-tanẓura maʿshūqī wa-narūḥa baʿda dhālika ilā maʿshūqatika
sentences.l: So-descend with-me so-that-you-look-at my-beloved, and-(that) we-go after that to your-beloved.
sentences.i: Come down with me and see my beloved, and afterwards we will go on to yours.”
sentences.n: inḥadara, Form VII, “to go down, descend”. li-tanẓura, “so that you may look”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, and narūḥa, “we go”, carries on in the same mood. rāḥa, “to go”, is the everyday verb of motion in this Arabic.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا دَهْنَشُ السَّمْعُ وَالطَّاعَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Dahnashu al-samʿu wa-al-ṭāʿatu
sentences.l: So-said to-her Dahnash: The-hearing and-the-obedience.
sentences.i: Dahnash said to her, “Hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: al-samʿu wa-al-ṭāʿatu, “hearing and obedience (are yours)”, the set reply of a servant who accepts a command.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ انْحَدَرَا إِلَى أَسْفَلَ فَنَزَلَا فِي دَوْرِ الْقَاعَةِ الَّتِي فِى الْبُرْجِ
sentences.tr: thumma inḥadarā ilā asfala fa-nazalā fī dawri al-qāʿati allatī fī al-burji
sentences.l: Then the-two-descended to below, and-the-two-alighted in (the) floor (of) the-hall which (is) in the-tower.
sentences.i: Then the two of them flew down and alighted within the hall in the tower.
sentences.n: inḥadarā and nazalā are dual, “the two of them”. ilā asfala, “to below, downwards”: asfal, “lower”, is a diptote and takes -a after ilā. dawr is “storey, floor of a building”, as it still is in Egypt; dawr al-qāʿa is probably the floor or level of the hall. فى here is the print's spelling of fī, “in”, with alif maqṣūra; both spellings occur on these pages.

sentences.t: وَأَوْقَفَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ دَهْنَشًا بِجَنْبِ السَّرِيرِ وَمَدَّتْ يَدَهَا وَشَالَتْ مُلَاءَةَ الْحَرِيرِ عَنْ وَجْهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-awqafat Maymūnatu Dahnashan bi-janbi al-sarīri wa-maddat yadahā wa-shālat mulāʾata al-ḥarīri ʿan wajhi Qamari al-Zamāni ibni al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: And-made-stand Maymūna Dahnash at-(the)-side (of) the-bed, and-she-stretched-out her-hand and-she-lifted (the) sheet (of) the-silk off (the) face (of) Qamar al-Zamān, son (of) the-king Shahramān.
sentences.i: Maymūna set Dahnash beside the bed, put out her hand and lifted the silken sheet from the face of Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān.
sentences.n: awqafa, Form IV, “to make (someone) stand”. Here the print writes دهنشا with the alif of the indefinite accusative, Dahnashan, as if the name were not a diptote; elsewhere on these pages it is not. bi-janbi, “at the side of”: bi- of place. The print itself marks the shadda of مدّت. shāla, “to lift, take up”, is a colloquial verb, Classical shāla meaning “to rise”; it is the everyday word in Egypt and Syria. mulāʾa, “sheet, wrapper”; the ء is printed.

sentences.t: فَسَطَعَ وَجْهُهُ وَلَمَعَ وَأَشْرَقَ وَزَهَى
sentences.tr: fa-saṭaʿa wajhuhu wa-lamaʿa wa-ashraqa wa-zahā
sentences.l: And-shone-out his-face, and-it-gleamed, and-it-beamed, and-it-glowed.
sentences.i: And his face blazed out, gleaming, beaming and glowing.
sentences.n: Four near-synonyms in a row, for effect: saṭaʿa, “to rise, spread (of light)”; lamaʿa, “to glitter”; ashraqa, “to shine, rise (of the sun)”; zahā, “to shine, be bright”.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ إِلَيْهِ وَالْتَفَتَتْ مِنْ وَقْتِهَا وَسَاعَتِهَا إِلَى دَهْنَشَ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ انْظُرْ يَا مَلْعُونُ وَلَا تَكُنْ أَقْبَحَ مَجْنُونٍ فَنَحْنُ بَنَاتٌ وَبِهِ مَفْتُونَاتٌ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat Maymūnatu ilayhi wa-iltafatat min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā ilā Dahnasha wa-qālat lahu unẓur yā malʿūnu wa-lā takun aqbaḥa majnūnin fa-naḥnu banātun wa-bihi maftūnātun
sentences.l: And-looked Maymūna at-him, and-she-turned from her-time and-her-hour to Dahnash, and-she-said to-him: Look, O cursed-one, and-not be (the) ugliest madman! For-we (are) girls, and-by-him (are) enchanted-ones.
sentences.i: Maymūna looked at him, then turned at once to Dahnash and said, “Look, you damned wretch, and don't be the most hideous of madmen! We are only girls, and we are bewitched by him.”
sentences.n: min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā, “from her time and her hour”, that is, then and there. Her words fall in rhymed prose: malʿūn / majnūn, banāt / maftūnāt. aqbaḥa majnūnin, “the ugliest of madmen”: an elative before an indefinite noun means “the most … of”; aqbaḥa is accusative as the predicate of takun. maftūn, “seduced, bewitched”, from fatana; bihi, “by him”, puts the cause first.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ نَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ دَهْنَشُ وَاسْتَمَرَّ بِتَأَمُّلٍ فِيهِ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika naẓara ilayhi Dahnashu wa-istamarra bi-taʾammulin fīhi sāʿatan
sentences.l: And-at that looked at-him Dahnash, and-he-continued with-contemplating in-him an-hour.
sentences.i: At that Dahnash looked at him, and went on gazing at him for a while.
sentences.n: istamarra bi-taʾammulin fīhi, “he kept on contemplating him”: istamarra, “to continue”, with bi- and a verbal noun, where Classical prose would write istamarra yataʾammalu. The print could also be a misprint for يتأمّل, “gazing”, differing by one dot; the sense is the same. taʾammala fī, “to look closely at, contemplate”. The print itself marks the shadda of استمرّ and تأمّل; the أ is printed. sāʿa is “an hour”, often just “a while”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَرَّكَ رَأْسَهُ وَقَالَ لِمَيْمُونَةَ وَاللّٰهِ يَا سَيِّدَتِي إِنَّكِ مَعْذُورَةٌ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥarraka raʾsahu wa-qāla li-Maymūnata wa-Allāhi yā sayyidatī innaki maʿdhūratun
sentences.l: Then he-moved his-head and-said to-Maymūna: By-God, O my-lady, indeed-you (are) excused.
sentences.i: Then he shook his head and said to Maymūna, “By God, my lady, you are not to be blamed.
sentences.n: The shadda of حرّك is the print's own, and the أ of رأسه is printed. wa-Allāhi, “by God”, the wāw of oaths, with the genitive. maʿdhūra, “excused”: your passion is pardonable.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ بَقِيَ عَلَيْكِ شَيْءٌ آخَرُ وَهُوَ أَنَّ حَالَ الْأُنْثَى غَيْرُ حَالِ الذَّكَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin baqiya ʿalayki shayʾun ākharu wa-huwa anna ḥāla al-unthā ghayru ḥāli al-dhakari
sentences.l: But there-remains upon-you a-thing other, and-it (is) that (the) state (of) the-female (is) other-than (the) state (of) the-male.
sentences.i: But there is one more thing you have yet to reckon with: a woman's case is not a man's.
sentences.n: baqiya ʿalayki, “there remains (owing) upon you”: one point still to be settled. ḥāl, “state, condition”: a girl's beauty is one thing and a youth's another, so the two cannot simply be ranked. The madda of آخر is printed.

sentences.t: وَحَقِّ اللّٰهِ إِنَّ مَعْشُوقَكِ هٰذَا أَشْبَهُ الْخَلْقِ بِمَعْشُوقَتِي فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ وَالْبَهْجَةِ وَالْكَمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaqqi Allāhi inna maʿshūqaki hādhā ashbahu al-khalqi bi-maʿshūqatī fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli wa-al-bahjati wa-al-kamāli
sentences.l: And-(by the) right (of) God, indeed your-beloved this (is the) most-resembling (of) the-creation to-my-beloved in the-beauty and-the-loveliness and-the-radiance and-the-perfection.
sentences.i: By God's truth, this beloved of yours is, of all creatures, the most like my own beloved, in beauty and loveliness, in radiance and perfection.
sentences.n: wa-ḥaqqi Allāhi, “by the right of God”, an oath with the wāw and the genitive. The shadda of اللّه is the print's own. ashbahu al-khalqi bi-, “the most like, of all creation, to”: ashbah is the elative of shabīh, and shabaha takes bi- for the thing one resembles. The rhyme falls on jamāl / kamāl.

sentences.t: وَهُمَا الِاثْنَانِ كَأَنَّهُمَا قَدْأُ فْرِغَا فِي قَالَبِ الْجَمَالِ سَوَاءً
sentences.tr: wa-humā al-ithnāni ka-annahumā qad ufrighā fī qālabi al-jamāli sawāʾan
sentences.l: And-they-two, the-two-of-them, as-if-they had been-poured in (the) mould (of) the-beauty, equally.
sentences.i: The pair of them are as if they had been cast in beauty's mould alike.”
sentences.n: The print sets قد افرغا, “they had been poured”, as قدا فرغا, the alif of the verb drawn back onto qad. The spacing is kept and pointed across the break: read qad ufrighā, Form IV passive of afragha, “to pour (molten metal)”, dual. ufrigha fī qālab, “poured into a mould”, is a stock image for perfect form. humā al-ithnāni, “they, the two of them”, is redundant, for emphasis. sawāʾan, “equally, alike”; the ء is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ مِنْ دَهْنَشَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِهَا ظَلَامًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Maymūnatu min Dahnasha hādhā al-kalāma ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihā ẓalāman
sentences.l: And-when heard Maymūna from Dahnash this the-speech, became the-light in her-face darkness.
sentences.i: When Maymūna heard these words from Dahnash, the light in her face turned to darkness.
sentences.n: ṣāra, “to become”, works like kāna, with its predicate, ẓalāman, “darkness”, in the accusative. ḍiyāʾ / ẓalām: the light of her face and the dark of her anger.

sentences.t: وَلَطَمَتْهُ بِجَنَاحِهَا عَلَى رَأْسِهِ لَطْمَةً قَوِيَّةً كَادَتْ أَنْ تَقْضِىَ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ شِدَّتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-laṭamathu bi-janāḥihā ʿalā raʾsihi laṭmatan qawiyyatan kādat an taqḍiya ʿalayhi min shiddatihā
sentences.l: And-she-struck-him with-her-wing on his-head a-blow strong; it-nearly (did) that it-finish-off him from its-force.
sentences.i: She struck him on the head with her wing, a blow so violent it nearly finished him off.
sentences.n: laṭama, “to slap, strike with the flat”, with laṭmatan as an absolute object, “struck him a blow”; bi-, “with”, names the instrument. kādat an, “it nearly”: kāda with an and the subjunctive. qaḍā ʿalā, “to put an end to, kill”: the verb takes ʿalā. The print spells taqḍiya with final ى for ي. The shadda of شدّتها is the print's own, and the أ of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ قَسَمًا بِنُورِ وَجْهِ جَلَالِهِ أَنْ تَرُوحَ يَا مَلْعُونُ فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ وَتَحْمِلَ مَعْشُوقَتَكَ الَّتِي تُحِبُّهَا وَتَأْتِيَ بِهَا سَرِيعًا إِلَى هٰذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu qasaman bi-nūri wajhi jalālihi an tarūḥa yā malʿūnu fī hādhihi al-sāʿati wa-taḥmila maʿshūqataka allatī tuḥibbuhā wa-taʾtiya bihā sarīʿan ilā hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: (I swear) an-oath by-(the)-light (of the) face (of) His-majesty, that you-go, O cursed-one, in this the-hour and-carry your-beloved whom you-love-her and-bring her quickly to this the-place,
sentences.i: And she said to him, “I swear by the light of the face of His majesty, you will go this very hour, you damned wretch, and carry off the beloved you love, and bring her here at once,
sentences.n: qasaman, “(I swear) an oath”, an absolute object standing for its verb; bi- is the bi- of oaths, “by”. jalālihi, “His majesty”, is God's: the pronoun is left without a named antecedent, as in pious formulas. an tarūḥa …, “that you go”: what she swears to is put as an and the subjunctive, in effect a command. atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb takes bi- for what is brought. The shadda of تحبّها is the print's own; the أ of تأتي is printed.

sentences.t: حَتَّى نَجْمَعَ بَيْنَ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَنَنْظُرَ فِيهِمَا وَهُمَا نَائِمَانِ بِالْقُرْبِ مِنْ بَعْضِهِمَا سَوَاءً فَيَظْهَرَ لَنَا أَيُّهُمَا أَمْلَحُ وَأَحْسَنُ مِنْ صَاحِبِهِ
sentences.tr: ḥattā najmaʿa bayna al-ithnayni wa-nanẓura fīhimā wa-humā nāʾimāni bi-al-qurbi min baʿḍihimā sawāʾan fa-yaẓhara lanā ayyuhumā amlaḥu wa-aḥsanu min ṣāḥibihi
sentences.l: so-that we-bring-together between the-two and-we-look into-them-both while-they-two (are) sleeping-ones in-the-nearness of each-other, alike, and-(so) it-appears to-us which-of-them (is) prettier and-more-beautiful than his-fellow.
sentences.i: so that we may lay the two side by side and look them over as they sleep close together, and see which of them is the prettier and the more beautiful of the pair.
sentences.n: jamaʿa bayna, “to bring together”. naẓara fī, “to examine, look into”. bi-al-qurbi min, “near to”: bi- of place. baʿḍihimā, “each other”, literally “some of the two”, the usual Middle Arabic reciprocal. fa-yaẓhara, subjunctive after fa- in the chain of purpose. ayyuhumā, “which of the two”: the print itself marks its shadda. ṣāḥib, “companion”, here simply “the other one”. The ئ of نائمان is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ مَا أَمَرْتُكَ بِهِ فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَهِ يَا مَلْعُونُ أَحْرَقْتُكَ بِنَارِي وَرَمَيْتُ عَلَيْكَ شَرَارِي وَمَزَّقْتُكَ قِطَعًا قِطَعًا وَأَرْمِيكَ فِى الْبَرَارِي وَأَجْعَلُكَ عِبْرَةً لِلْمُقِيمِ وَالسَّارِي
sentences.tr: wa-in lam tafʿal mā amartuka bihi fī hādhihi al-sāʿahi yā malʿūnu aḥraqtuka bi-nārī wa-ramaytu ʿalayka sharārī wa-mazzaqtuka qiṭaʿan qiṭaʿan wa-armīka fī al-barārī wa-ajʿaluka ʿibratan li-al-muqīmi wa-al-sārī
sentences.l: And-if not you-do what I-commanded-you with-it in this the-hour, O cursed-one, I-burn-you with-my-fire and-I-throw upon-you my-sparks and-I-tear-you pieces pieces, and-I-throw-you in the-wastes, and-I-make-you a-lesson for-the-one-staying and-the-one-travelling-by-night.
sentences.i: And if you do not do as I have bidden you this very hour, you damned wretch, I will burn you with my fire and shower my sparks upon you, tear you to pieces and fling you into the wilderness, and make of you an example to all who stay at home and all who travel by night.”
sentences.n: The threat runs in rhymed prose on -ārī: nārī / sharārī / al-barārī / al-sārī. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes bi- for the thing commanded, so mā amartuka bihi is “what I commanded you (to do)”. After in, the perfects aḥraqtuka, ramaytu and mazzaqtuka have future sense, “I shall burn you …”; then the imperfects armīka and ajʿaluka carry on in the same sense. The print spells al-sāʿa here with ه for ة. qiṭaʿan qiṭaʿan, “piece by piece, to pieces”: the doubling distributes. barārī, plural of barriyya, “desert, open country”. li-al-muqīmi wa-al-sārī, “for the settled and the night-traveller”: for everyone, as a pair of opposites. The shadda of مزّقتك is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا دَهْنَشُ يَاسَيِّدَتِي لَكِ عَلَيَّ ذٰلِكَ وَأَنَا أَعْرِفُ أَنَّ مَحْبُوبَتِي أَمْلَحُ وَأَحْلَى
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Dahnashu yā-sayyidatī laki ʿalayya dhālika wa-anā aʿrifu anna maḥbūbatī amlaḥu wa-aḥlā
sentences.l: So-said to-her Dahnash: O-my-lady, for-you (is) upon-me that; and-I know that my-beloved (is) prettier and-sweeter.
sentences.i: Dahnash said to her, “My lady, you have my word on it; and I know that my beloved is the prettier and the sweeter.”
sentences.n: The print has ملّي, a misprint for عليّ, corrected here. laki ʿalayya dhālika, “that is yours, binding upon me”: a promise. ياسيدتي is printed as one word, yā sayyidatī, “O my lady”. The kasra of لكِ is the print's own: it marks the feminine “to you”. maḥbūba, “beloved”, a second word for what he has been calling maʿshūqa; amlaḥ and aḥlā are elatives of malīḥ, “pretty”, and ḥulw, “sweet”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ دَهْنَشَ طَارَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَطَارَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ مَعَهُ مِنْ أَجْلِ الْمُحَافَظَةِ عَلَيْهِ فَغَابَا سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿifrīta Dahnasha ṭāra min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-ṭārat Maymūnatu maʿahu min ajli al-muḥāfaẓati ʿalayhi fa-ghābā sāʿatan zamāniyyatan
sentences.l: Then indeed the-ifrit Dahnash flew from his-time and-his-hour, and-flew Maymūna with-him for (the) sake (of) the-keeping-watch over-him; and-the-two-were-absent an-hour of-time.
sentences.i: Then the ifrit Dahnash flew off then and there, and Maymūna flew with him to keep an eye on him, and the two were gone for a full hour.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, a common way of moving the story on. After inna the name is accusative; written without alif here, it is read as a diptote, Dahnasha. min ajli, “for the sake of, in order to”. ḥāfaẓa ʿalā, “to watch over, guard”: she goes along to make sure he does not cheat. sāʿa zamāniyya, “an hour of time”: a real hour by the clock, as against sāʿa, “a while”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَقْبَلَ الِاثْنَانِ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ وَهُمَا حَامِلَانِ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةَ وَعَلَيْهَا قَمِيصٌ بُنْدُ قِيٌّ رَفِيعٌ بِطِرَازَيْنِ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَهُوَ مُزَرْكَشٌ بِبَدَائِعِ التَّطْرِيزَاتِ
sentences.tr: thumma aqbala al-ithnāni baʿda dhālika wa-humā ḥāmilāni tilka al-ṣabiyyata wa-ʿalayhā qamīṣun bunduqiyyun rafīʿun bi-ṭirāzayni mina al-dhahabi wa-huwa muzarkashun bi-badāʾiʿi al-taṭrīzāti
sentences.l: Then came the-two after that, and-they-two (were) carrying that the-girl, and-on-her a-shift Venetian fine with-two-embroidered-bands of the-gold, and-it (was) brocaded with-(the)-marvels (of) the-embroideries.
sentences.i: After that the two of them came back carrying the girl. She wore a shift of fine Venetian stuff with two borders of gold, worked all over with marvels of embroidery,
sentences.n: aqbala, “to come forward, arrive”, singular before its dual subject, as a verb that comes first normally is. ḥāmilāni, “carrying”, dual active participle with an object. بند قي is printed as two words: bunduqī, “Venetian”, from al-Bunduqiyya, “Venice”, a byword for fine imported cloth; it is pointed across the break. ṭirāz, a band of embroidery or woven inscription on a garment, here dual, “two bands”. muzarkash, “brocaded, embroidered with gold thread”, a Persian-derived word. badāʾiʿ, “marvels, rare and wonderful things”, plural of badīʿa; the ئ is printed.

sentences.t: وَرَأْسُ الْكُمَّيْنِ مَكْتُوبٌ عَلَيْهِ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-raʾsu al-kummayni maktūbun ʿalayhi hādhihi al-abyātu shiʿrun
sentences.l: and-(the) head (of) the-two-sleeves, written on-it (were) these the-verses — verse:
sentences.i: and on the cuffs of the two sleeves these lines were written:
sentences.n: raʾs al-kummayn, “the head of the two sleeves”, the cuff ends; kumm, “sleeve”, here dual. maktūbun ʿalayhi …, “written upon it (are) these verses”: the passive participle is masculine singular because it comes first. The أ of رأس is printed. شعر, “verse”, is the print's rubric announcing the poem.

sentences.t:
ثَلَثَةٌ مَنَعَتْهَا عَنْ زِيَارَتِنَا * خَوْفُ الرَّقِيبِ وَخَوْفُ الْحَاسِدِ الْخَنِقِ
ضَوْءُ الْجَبِينِ وَوَسْوَاسُ الْحُلِيِّ وَمَا * حَوَتْ مَعَاطِفُهَا مِنْ عَنْبَرٍ عَبِقِ
هَبِ الْجَبِينَ بِفَضْلِ الْكُمِّ تَسْتُرُهُ * وَالْحَلْيُ تَنْزِعُهُ مَا حِيلَةُ الْعَرَقِ
sentences.tr:
thalāthatun manaʿathā ʿan ziyāratinā * khawfu al-raqībi wa-khawfu al-ḥāsidi al-khaniqi
ḍawʾu al-jabīni wa-waswāsu al-ḥuliyyi wa-mā * ḥawat maʿāṭifuhā min ʿanbarin ʿabiqi
habi al-jabīna bi-faḍli al-kummi tasturuhu * wa-al-ḥalyu tanziʿuhu mā ḥīlatu al-ʿaraqi
sentences.l:
Three (things) kept-her from visiting-us, * (the) fear (of) the-watcher and-(the) fear (of) the-envier, the-choking-with-rage:
(the) light (of) the-brow, and-(the) whisper (of) the-ornaments, and-what * held her-folds of ambergris fragrant.
Grant the-brow, with-(the)-excess (of) the-sleeve she-veils-it, * and-the-ornament she-strips-it-off: what (is the) remedy (for) the-sweat?
sentences.i:
Three things kept her from visiting us, for fear of the watcher and of the envier, choking with spite:
the light of her brow, the whisper of her ornaments, and the fragrant ambergris that her garments' folds hold close.
Grant that she veils her brow with the trailing sleeve, and takes her ornaments off: what can she do about her sweat?
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ, rhyming in -iqi. The pointing is the print's own. ثلثة is the edition's spelling of thalātha, “three”, without the long alif, and is pointed as written. The three things that would betray her on her way to the lover are named in the second line; the first line gives the reason she fears betrayal, the watcher (raqīb) and the envier, stock figures of love poetry. khawfu is pointed as a nominative, where the sense invites the accusative of reason, khawfa, “for fear of”; it is kept. al-khaniqi, as printed, is “choking (with rage)”, from khaniqa, “to be choked”; the line is often quoted with al-ḥaniqi, “the rancorous”, which differs by one dot, and either fits. waswās, “whisper, faint rustle”, is the tinkle of her jewellery; ḥuliyy is the plural of ḥaly, “ornament”, which comes in the singular in the last line. maʿāṭif, “sides, folds (of a garment)”. hab, imperative of wahaba, “to give”, used as “grant that, suppose”. faḍl al-kumm is the part of the sleeve that hangs beyond the hand. The last question is the point: her very sweat is scented with ambergris and gives her away. The lines are embroidered on the sleeves, and they name a sleeve.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ دَهْنَشُ وَمَيْمُونَةُ حَامِلَيْنِ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةَ حَتَّى وَضَعَاهَا وَمَدَّاهَا بِجَانِبِ الْغُلَامِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal Dahnashu wa-Maymūnatu ḥāmilayni tilka al-ṣabiyyata ḥattā waḍaʿāhā wa-maddāhā bi-jānibi al-ghulāmi Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-not ceased Dahnash and-Maymūna (being) two-carrying that the-girl, until the-two-set-her-down and-the-two-stretched-her-out at-(the)-side (of) the-youth Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Dahnash and Maymūna carried the girl on until they set her down and laid her out beside the youth Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “did not cease”, works like kāna, with its predicate in the accusative: ḥāmilayni, “carrying”, dual. The verb is singular because it comes before its subjects. madda, “to stretch out”, here “to lay at full length”; the print itself marks the shadda of مدّاها. bi-jānibi, “beside”: bi- of place.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
